valley/map: Here is f, a function of two weights, w zero and w one: numbers that a program tunes as it learns. Seen from above, each ring joins points of equal height.
valley/valley: The rings make a long, narrow valley: steep from wall to wall, and nearly flat along the floor.
valley/descent: Gradient descent walks down it, one gradient step after another, each moving w by minus eta times the gradient.
valley/zig: Across the valley the walls are steep, so each step overshoots to the far wall: a zigzag.
valley/crawl: Along the floor the slope is gentle, so the steps are short, and the walk crawls.
trap/split: Why not take bigger steps? Each direction is a bowl of its own: across, its steepness, A, is one; along, just zero point zero five.
trap/across: With eta at zero point nine, the step factor across, one minus two A eta, is minus zero point eight: the sign flips every step.
trap/along: Along, the factor is zero point nine one: each step leaves ninety-one percent of the way to go.
trap/cap: And eta cannot pass one over A across, which is one, or the zigzag blows up: the steep side caps the step for both.
ball/heavy: Boris Polyak, a mathematician in Moscow, noted in 1964 that most functions look like this near their lowest point, and took a fix from physics: a heavy ball rolling down this valley keeps its motion, and runs along the floor.
ball/name: He called it the heavy ball method. Its usual name, momentum, is the physicist's word for the motion a moving mass carries.
ball/velocity: So keep the last move as a vector, v, the velocity: how far, and which way, the weights went last step.
ball/keep: Each step, the velocity keeps a share of itself, mu, the Greek letter mu: here, a half.
ball/push: Then it adds the usual push, minus eta g. Alone, the push lands high on the far wall; the kept half pulls it back down, and farther along.
ball/rule: Together, v gets mu v minus eta g. Then the weights move by the velocity: w gets w plus v.
ball/zero: Mu sets how much motion survives a step, like one minus friction. At zero, this is plain gradient descent.
ball/half: At a half, with the same eta, the zigzag dies in a few steps, and the ball runs far ahead.
build/one: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams used momentum in 1986 to make programs learn faster; in one example, mu was zero point nine and eta zero point one. Take those for a single weight, w, at one, with a gradient of two.
build/v1: From rest, v is zero, so the first velocity is just minus zero point one times two: minus zero point two, a plain step.
build/w1: So w, which was one, becomes zero point eight.
build/v2: The gradient is two again. The velocity keeps zero point nine of minus zero point two, and adds another minus zero point two: minus zero point three eight.
build/w2: So this step is almost twice as long: w, at zero point eight, becomes zero point four two.
build/steady: Keep the gradient steady, and the pushes pile up in v, each adding a little less.
build/settle: It levels off where a step no longer changes it: where v equals zero point nine v, minus zero point two.
build/solve: Take zero point nine v from both sides: zero point one v is minus zero point two, so v is minus two: ten times a plain step.
build/limit: With any mu, the same steps give v approaches minus eta g, over one minus mu, the arrow read “approaches”: one over one minus mu, times a plain step.
build/flip: Across the valley, though, the gradient flips sign every step: each push undoes the last inside v, and the zigzag is damped.
